result.summary: This unit is the surface of golang.org/x/sys/windows: DLL loading and proc-call plumbing, syscall declarations, security/token/service/setupapi wrappers, and type and constant definitions. I checked load-time initialisation, linkname use, dynamic function-pointer calls, and every file for hidden network activity, encoded payloads or environment-dependent behaviour. All of it matches the expected upstream Go project code. Nothing runs on its own beyond obtaining the standard handles, and every OS interaction is a thin wrapper invoked by the caller.

findings.title: Documented DLL preloading risk in LoadDLL/NewLazyDLL
findings.detail: LoadDLL and NewLazyDLL accept non-absolute names and are subject to DLL search-order hijacking. This is upstream behaviour and documented in the source; NewLazySystemDLL restricts loading to System32. It is a caller-side concern, not deliberate.

findings.title: Package-level variable initialisation calls GetStdHandle
findings.detail: The only load-time side effect is the package-level initialisation of Stdin/Stdout/Stderr via GetStdHandle. This is benign and matches upstream. There is no init() function, no hooking or patching, and no embedded or encoded data.

capabilities.explanation: This is the package's core mechanism for calling Windows APIs. LazyDLL/DLL.FindProc resolve function addresses with GetProcAddress, and Proc.Call/LazyProc.Call invoke them through syscall.SyscallN. connectEx, WSASendMsg and WSARecvMsg call function pointers obtained via WSAIoctl(SIO_GET_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_POINTER), and NewCallback converts Go funcs into stdcall pointers. All targets are system DLL exports named in the source (generated //sys stubs) or chosen by the caller. Nothing loads or runs code from data.
